bibliography.abstract: Abstract Urban street reallocations and redesigns are central to sustainable mobility transitions, yet public acceptance remains a major challenge. While previous research has examined general attitudes toward transport policy, little is known about how specific design features shape support across diverse user groups. We conducted a large-scale stated choice experiment (N = 5991) embedded in a nationally representative mobility panel in Switzerland. Respondents evaluated navigable 360° and static visualizations of redesigned fictional urban streets, varying in infrastructure, greenery, and social space. We examine effects on three outcome dimensions: acceptance, willingness to live nearby, and willingness to cycle. Greenery consistently increases support across both formats. How the redesigns are visualized shapes which features become salient: the 360° condition increases sensitivity to social features, while the static condition increases sensitivity to environmental and infrastructural features. Subgroup analyses reveal substantial cleavages by gender, age, transport behavior, and political ideology. The results show that design-sensitive, visually supported planning strategies can build broader public coalitions for urban street transformations. Our findings inform participatory planning and policy design for more inclusive and context-sensitive urban transitions.

bibliography.title: Space for people, not cars: a large-scale visual choice experiment on urban street redesigns

orgs.label: Institute of Urban and Regional Development

en.caveats: The study relies on stated preferences and fictional street designs rather than real-world behavioral responses to actual street reallocations.
en.what: A stated choice experiment with 5,991 participants from a representative Swiss mobility panel evaluated fictional urban street redesigns using either static images or navigable 360-degree visualizations. The experiment varied street infrastructure, social spaces, and greenery to measure their impact on public acceptance, willingness to live nearby, and willingness to cycle. The 360-degree format made social features more salient to respondents, while static images heightened sensitivity to environmental and infrastructural elements.
en.why: It demonstrates that the choice of visualization medium directly biases how the public evaluates street redesigns, while also showing that adding greenery is a universally effective strategy to boost public acceptance across diverse demographic and political groups.
